title: The Periodic Table of Elements
competency: Discuss the significant contributions of early scientists in the development of the periodic table; identify the names and symbols of the first 20 or several common elements; explain the arrangement of elements into 7 periods and 18 groups; calculate the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom; and explain the role of valence electrons.
objectives: Trace the historical development of the periodic table.
Identify the names and symbols of the first 20 elements.
Describe the arrangement of the periodic table in terms of groups and periods.
Calculate the number of subatomic particles using atomic number and mass number.
Explain how an element's position is determined by its electron structure and valence electrons.
introduction: The Periodic Table is more than just a chart; it is a map of the building blocks of the universe. It organizes all known elements in a way that reveals patterns in their properties. By understanding its layout, scientists can predict how elements will react with one another.
content:
1. Brief History of the Periodic Table

  • Johann Döbereiner (1817): Grouped elements into 'Triads' with similar properties.
  • John Newlands (1864): Proposed the 'Law of Octaves,' noting that properties repeat every eighth element.
  • Dmitri Mendeleev (1869): Created the first widely accepted periodic table, arranging elements by increasing atomic mass and leaving gaps for undiscovered elements.
  • Henry Moseley (1913): Reorganized the table by increasing atomic number, which is the basis of the Modern Periodic Table.

2. Organization: Periods and Groups

  • Periods (Horizontal Rows): There are 7 periods. Elements in the same period have the same number of occupied electron shells.
  • Groups/Families (Vertical Columns): There are 18 groups. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.

3. Calculating Subatomic Particles

To find the composition of an atom, we use these formulas:

  • Atomic Number (Z) = Number of Protons = Number of Electrons (in a neutral atom).
  • Mass Number (A) = Protons + Neutrons.
  • Number of Neutrons = Mass Number - Atomic Number.

4. Valence Electrons and Position

Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell. They determine how an element reacts. For example, Group 1 elements have 1 valence electron and are highly reactive metals, while Group 18 elements have a full outer shell and are non-reactive (Noble Gases).

examples.title: Calculations for Aluminum (Al)
examples.description: Aluminum has an Atomic Number of 13 and a Mass Number of 27. Therefore: Protons = 13, Electrons = 13, Neutrons = 27 - 13 = 14.

examples.title: First 20 Elements
examples.description: H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar, K, Ca.

keyTerms.definition: A horizontal row in the periodic table.
A vertical column in the periodic table, also known as a family.
Electrons found in the outermost energy level of an atom.

keyConcepts: The modern periodic table is arranged by increasing atomic number.
Elements in the same group share similar chemical behaviors.
The number of valence electrons determines an element's reactivity and its group number (for main-group elements).
summary: The Periodic Table has evolved from Mendeleev’s mass-based arrangement to Moseley’s atomic number-based system. It is organized into 7 periods and 18 groups. By using the atomic and mass numbers, we can calculate subatomic particles, while valence electrons dictate the chemical identity and reactivity of each element.
